## Where This Fits
The second week of Part II. W7 decided how many tokens to buy and which ones; up to there, W1's table of where a capability can come from had one entry ticked — **the pre-training distribution**. This week opens the second: **human demonstrations**, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) — continued training of a compressor that has read some fifteen trillion tokens on between a thousand and a million written exchanges (LIMA used 1,000; the Tülu 3 SFT mixture has about 940,000). The week asks four things. **First, what it learns.** Every detail of the data format — the chat template, computing the loss on the response only, the end-of-sequence token, packing — comes with "what goes wrong if you get it wrong"; and the 2023–2024 evidence points one way: SFT mostly changes **which sub-distribution the model samples from and in what format it answers** (LIMA's superficial alignment hypothesis; URIAL measures that base and aligned models diverge at only a small share of token positions, mostly stylistic ones), while teaching new facts through SFT is slow and, once learned, raises hallucination (Gekhman et al.) — new knowledge comes from pre-training (W7) or retrieval (W12). **Second, how to train on a machine it does not fit.** W4 counted one parameter at 16 bytes: full fine-tuning of an 8B model needs 128 GB, against 64 GB on the demo machine and 16 GB on the project GPU. Freezing the weights and learning only a low-rank correction — LoRA, $\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{W}_0 + s\,\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}$ — is the **third** low-rank factorisation of the course: W1's SGNS was low rank that training produced, W3's MLA used low rank to shrink the **state** carried at inference, and this week uses it to shrink the **update** learned in training; QLoRA then stores the frozen copy in 4 bits. For the first time three numbers go on the same ledger: for an 8B model, full fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA need roughly 131, 17 and 5–7 GB before any activations — and what LoRA saves is neither the weights nor the activations but the frozen weights' gradients, master copy and two moments; its FLOPs fall by only about a third, because the backward pass still has to walk all the way back. **Third, is what you save the same thing?** This is the week of the course most dense in methodology: LoRA and full fine-tuning leave weights with different spectral structure (intruder dimensions, NeurIPS 2025); LoRA learns less and forgets less (TMLR 2024); and once the learning rate is tuned for each, nine recent LoRA variants come within 1–2% of vanilla LoRA (Lee et al. 2026, a workshop paper) — consistent with Thinking Machines' blog post (LoRA's optimal learning rate is about ten times full fine-tuning's, and it should be applied to every layer, the MLP above all; **not peer-reviewed**). It is the best case in the course for the first reading question — was the baseline's learning rate tuned? — and the reason for this week's assigned reading; the strength of both pieces of evidence is part of the lesson. **Fourth, what it costs, how to measure it, and how to pay less.** Catastrophic forgetting is the price of the second entry: W1's bits-per-byte ruler measures the model before and after SFT, on W1's Traditional Chinese passage among others; W2's vocabulary extension plus continued pre-training returns here (new embeddings start from nothing, forgetting follows, and learning-rate re-warming plus replay is the baseline remedy); and "forgotten" does not always mean erased — part of it is task inference pushed aside, recoverable by asking differently; RL-style post-training forgets less than SFT, and both explanations on offer (the KL divergence from the base model, on-policy data) point to next week. The last part takes "one bypass per task" to its end: task arithmetic, TIES and DARE add separately trained corrections together, which works only from a shared pre-trained starting point — W4's residual stream is the shared coordinate system. **The memory and FLOP arithmetic is done live by the instructor and checked against peak memory measured on the demo machine; the before/after SFT comparison and the learning-rate sweep are rehearsed in advance and replayed; the singular-vector comparison runs live**; you do not need to run anything.

## Learning Objectives
1. Write a conversation out as a token sequence under a chat template and point on it to where $\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}$ is computed (the response and its end token, not the prompt), why control tokens and the end-of-sequence token must be learned, and why packing must separate attention and positions — and say what goes wrong in each case; say for which shapes of data computing the loss on the prompt too does better (Huerta-Enochian & Ko; Shi et al.) — so it is a hyperparameter to report, and mlx-lm's default is not to mask.
2. State what SFT mainly changes (which sub-distribution the model samples from and in what format — LIMA's superficial alignment hypothesis; URIAL's token-distribution shift concentrated on stylistic tokens) and the cost of teaching new facts through SFT (Gekhman et al.: learned slowly, and hallucination rises linearly once they are learned), and point, in demo 1's base-versus-SFT comparison, to which part changed.
3. Write the LoRA forward pass $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{W}_0\mathbf{x} + s\,\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$, count its trainable parameters $r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})$, split W4's 16 bytes per parameter into what LoRA saves (the frozen weights' gradient 2, master copy 4, two moments 8) and what it does not (the bf16 weights 2, the activations), compute full fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA for an 8B model and point to where demo 2's measured peak differs; and state that FLOPs per token fall from $6N$ to about $4N$, not to $2N$ — the backward pass still walks all the way back.
4. Explain why initialising $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$ makes training start exactly at the base model, why only $\mathbf{B}$ moves on the first step, and what happens if both are zero; say why the three ways of writing the scale $s$ (Hu's $\alpha/r$, rsLoRA's $\alpha/\sqrt{r}$, mlx-lm's plain `scale`) mean that "the same learning rate" is not the same thing across frameworks; and set LoRA beside W1's SGNS and W3's MLA: one low-rank factorisation, three uses (produced by training, shrinking a state, shrinking an update).
5. Explain what each of QLoRA's three components solves (NF4: a quantile grid for normally distributed weights; double quantization: quantizing the quantization constants, 0.5 → 0.127 bits per parameter; paged optimizers: paging optimizer state to the CPU when the GPU runs out), in what precision the arithmetic runs (stored in 4 bits, computed in bf16), and what "QLoRA" actually is on the demo machine (mlx's affine 4-bit base with bf16 adapters, not NF4; unified memory leaves nothing to page to).
6. State the two kinds of evidence that LoRA is not equivalent to full fine-tuning and how they complement each other (Shuttleworth et al.'s intruder dimensions — new directions among the fine-tuned weight's top-$k$ singular vectors, nearly orthogonal to every pre-trained singular vector, on which the forgetting concentrates; Biderman et al.'s learns less, forgets less); state the 2026 negative result (Lee et al.: with the learning rate tuned for each, nine variants come within 1–2% of vanilla) and the four claims of Schulman's blog post; say how strong each piece of evidence is (a workshop paper, a blog post, TMLR); and point, on demo 3's two learning-rate curves, to what is wrong with a comparison at one fixed learning rate.
7. Measure catastrophic forgetting (demo 4: the same bits-per-byte ruler before and after SFT, W1's Traditional Chinese passage included), separate three readings of it (genuinely overwritten — McCloskey & Cohen's interference; task inference pushed aside — Kotha et al.'s conjugate prompting, Zheng et al.'s spurious forgetting; plain drift — CapTrack), state the baseline remedy for continued pre-training (Ibrahim et al.: learning-rate re-warming and re-decaying plus replay) and the price of W2's vocabulary extension, and give the two explanations of why RL forgets less (Shenfeld et al.'s KL; Chen et al.'s on-policy data) — the way into W9.
8. Write task arithmetic, TIES and DARE (and why DARE's $1/(1-p)$ keeps the expectation), state their shared precondition (one pre-trained starting point; small, redundant corrections) and when they fail (sign conflicts; gains that shrink as tasks are added; weaker base models).

## Demos
The programs for this week's demos, published as they are built. **You are not required to run anything** — the numbers on the slides are the rehearsal records checked in with the code — but the code is published so that you can read it, re-run it, and change it. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment.

| | Slide | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|----------------------|-------|----------------------------------------------|---------------|----------|
| [**Demo 1**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w08_d1_sft_base_to_assistant)<br>[SFT turns a base model into an assistant]{.demo-sub} | p8–p9, p15, p42 | **Why:** the week's first question is what a thousand written answers teach a pre-trained model. Put the same three questions to a base model and to the same model after SFT, and look at one visible thing: does it stop, and on which token?<br>**What you see:** Qwen3-1.7B-Base, and LoRA adapters ($r = 16$, every linear layer of every block) trained on 1,000 instruction–answer pairs from Dolly 15k — A with the loss on the answer only, B with the loss on every token, C = A plus LoRA on the embedding rows. Three questions to each; one training example printed token by token with the positions that carry the loss; held-out loss on 200 examples; and the slide's one-line training command run for 12 steps.<br>**Result:** the base model already answers two of the three questions and stops — on the document's end token (`endoftext`). Adapters A and B learn the shape of the chat format but never stop: where the end-of-turn token (`im_end`) should be they emit untrained rare tokens, because LoRA inside the blocks cannot reach the embedding rows of tokens pre-training never produced. Adapter C stops on all three. Held-out response loss, nats per token: base 2.717, A 2.012, B 1.973, C 1.721. One model, one dataset, one seed, an untuned learning rate | `mlx`, `mlx-lm` at the pinned commit, `transformers`; about 3.4 GB of model | Apple silicon |
| [**Demo 2**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w08_d2_memory_ledger)<br>[The memory ledger: formula against measured peak]{.demo-sub} | p32–p33, p41 | **Why:** p25's ledger says what LoRA saves and what it does not. Put a real 8B model's shape into it, then run it and see what the formula leaves out.<br>**What you see:** (a) from Qwen3-8B's `config.json`: $N$ counted matrix by matrix, $N_{\text{LoRA}}$ for $r = 16$, and four rows — full fine-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA with two ways of storing 4 bits — against 64 GB and 16 GB. (b) the measured peak of `mlx-lm`'s training loop at 256 and 1,024 tokens, and at 1,024 with gradient checkpointing, for LoRA on the bf16 model, the same LoRA on the 4-bit model, and full fine-tuning of a 1.7B model; next to two formulas — the textbook's 16 bytes per trainable parameter, and what mlx actually stores.<br>**Result:** 131.1, 17.1, 6.8 and 5.3 GB; of LoRA's 17.1, the frozen weights are 16.4 — it does not fit in 16 GB because of the weights it does not train. Measured peaks: LoRA 20.1 and 30.3 GB, QLoRA 8.3 and 17.9: about 13 GB of activations per 1,000 tokens either way — 4-bit storage does not shrink them; checkpointing gives back 10.5 GB at 1.2× the time. mlx keeps Adam's moments in the weight's dtype and no fp32 master copy, so full fine-tuning of the 1.7B model peaks at 13.4–17.4 GB, below the textbook's 27.5; the price: after 20 steps 81 % of its weights are bit-for-bit unchanged | (a) standard library only; (b) `mlx`, `mlx-lm`; 16.4 GB for the bf16 8B model | (a) any laptop; (b) Apple silicon, 32 GB or more |
| [**Demo 3**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w08_d3_lr_sweep)<br>[Two learning-rate sweeps: LoRA and full fine-tuning]{.demo-sub} | p48–p49 | **Why:** p44–p47 argue that most "method A beats method B" tables compare one tuned method with one untuned one. Do the comparison properly once, at small scale.<br>**What you see:** demo 1's model and data; LoRA and full fine-tuning each trained at five learning rates (500 steps, same seed), the final held-out loss against the learning rate as two curves; then each method at the other's best learning rate, and LoRA at the rate you would get by copying a paper that writes the scale as $\alpha = 2r$.<br>**Result:** full fine-tuning has a clear U with its floor at $5 \times 10^{-6}$ (1.934); LoRA's curve is flatter, floor at $2.4 \times 10^{-6}$ (1.924). Each at its own best, they are 0.01 apart. The ratio of the two best rates is 0.48× in mlx's units and 4.8× in $\alpha = 2r$ units — the scale factor and the learning rate are tangled (p27), so "LoRA wants ten times the learning rate" depends on how the scale is written. Copying the rate across conventions costs LoRA 0.05 nats; giving full fine-tuning LoRA's best rate costs it 0.05 too. One seed; fourteen runs, about 1.6 hours | `mlx`, `mlx-lm`; demo 1's data | Apple silicon, 32 GB or more |
| [**Demo 4**](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w08_d4_intruders_forgetting)<br>[What the side road left behind: intruder dimensions and forgetting]{.demo-sub} | p54–p55, p58 | **Why:** Shuttleworth et al. report that LoRA's weights contain high-ranking singular directions unlike any pre-trained one. Count them in demo 3's two best runs — and then measure what either run forgot.<br>**What you see:** (a) the definition written live in a few lines of NumPy: SVD of a pre-trained matrix and of its fine-tuned version, and for each of the top 10 fine-tuned directions the largest cosine with any pre-trained one. (b) bits per byte — W1's ruler — of the base model, the LoRA model and the fully fine-tuned one on four held-out texts, among them a Traditional Chinese paragraph the English fine-tuning data never touched.<br>**Result:** (a) zero intruders, in every block and at every threshold: the update is too small — its largest singular value is under 6 % of the tenth singular value of the weight it is added to — so the top directions cannot change. The two updates still differ in shape: effective rank 16 for LoRA, about 1,900 of 2,048 for full fine-tuning. (b) on 1 MB of Wikipedia, 0.805 → 0.812 for both; the Chinese paragraph 1.050 → 1.051 and 1.052. By this ruler the fine-tuning cost under 1 %, LoRA and full alike, while the target loss fell from 2.72 to 1.92. A small model, a thousand examples, a small learning rate: the paper's effect is not reproduced here, and the slides say why | (a) `numpy`; (b) `mlx`, `mlx-lm`; demo 3's weights | (a) any laptop; (b) Apple silicon |

Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 27.2, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock`. "Any laptop" means the code depends on nothing platform-specific, not that it was verified elsewhere. Terminal prompts are in Chinese.

## References
- **Textbooks**: JM3 ch 8 *Post-training* (2026-08-19 release) — §8.1 Instruction Tuning and §8.2 Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning (LoRA) are this week; §8.3–8.4 (preferences, PPO, DPO) are W9; it has no section on QLoRA, chat templates, catastrophic forgetting or model merging (checked 2026-11-08), so the second half of this week has no textbook. Raschka, *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)*: ch 6 *Finetuning for Text Classification*, ch 7 *Finetuning to Follow Instructions*, Appendix E *Parameter-efficient Finetuning with LoRA*; Alammar & Grootendorst, *Hands-On Large Language Models*: ch 12 *Fine-Tuning Generation Models*.

**SFT: the data, the loss, and what it learns**
- Ouyang et al., **Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback**, NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2203.02155) — the abstract: the 1.3B InstructGPT is preferred to the 175B GPT-3; SFT is the first of three stages, and in the body its data are about 13k training prompts (Table 9: 12,725)
- Wei et al., **Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners**, ICLR 2022 Oral (arXiv:2109.01652) — FLAN; the abstract: a 137B model instruction-tuned on over 60 tasks beats zero-shot 175B GPT-3 on 20 of 25
- Zhou et al., **LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2305.11206) — the abstract: 65B LLaMa fine-tuned on only 1,000 curated prompts and responses; almost all knowledge is learned in pre-training; **the superficial alignment hypothesis is stated in §2**, not the abstract
- Lin et al., **The Unlocking Spell on Base LLMs: Rethinking Alignment via In-Context Learning**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2312.01552) — URIAL; the abstract: most distribution shifts between base and aligned models occur on stylistic tokens; three stylistic examples and a system prompt align a base model in context
- Gekhman et al., **Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?**, EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2405.05904; Anthology 2024.emnlp-main.444) — the abstract: examples with new knowledge are learned significantly more slowly and, once learned, linearly increase the tendency to hallucinate
- Lambert et al., **Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2411.15124) — a fully open post-training recipe; in the body (Table 7), 939,344 prompts in SFT
- Huerta-Enochian & Ko, **Instruction Fine-Tuning: Does Prompt Loss Matter?**, EMNLP 2024 (arXiv:2401.13586; Anthology 2024.emnlp-main.1267) — the abstract: on short-completion data, performance has a statistically significant negative quadratic relationship with the prompt loss weight; small values (0.01–0.5) do better on multiple-choice and short-generation benchmarks
- Shi et al., **Instruction Tuning With Loss Over Instructions**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2405.14394) — the abstract: applying the loss to the instruction too helps with long instructions, short outputs, or few examples
- Krell et al., **Efficient Sequence Packing without Cross-contamination: Accelerating Large Language Models without Impacting Performance**, arXiv:2107.02027 (v2 2022) — the abstract: up to half of the tokens in BERT pre-training data can be padding; in the body, a block-diagonal mask and position resets; **no peer-reviewed venue found**
- Kundu et al., **Enhancing Training Efficiency Using Packing with Flash Attention**, arXiv:2407.09105 (2024) — packing isolated through `position_ids` in Hugging Face Transformers 4.44; **a preprint**
- Ivison et al., **Large-Scale Data Selection for Instruction Tuning**, arXiv:2503.01807 (2025) — the abstract: when selecting up to 2.5M samples from pools of millions, many recently proposed methods fall short of random selection — "was the baseline compared?" on the data side; **a preprint**

**PEFT and LoRA**
- Houlsby et al., **Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP**, ICML 2019 (PMLR 97; arXiv:1902.00751) — adapters; the abstract: 3.6% added parameters per task, within 0.4% of full fine-tuning on GLUE; in the body, inserted after each sub-layer's output projection and before the residual add
- Li & Liang, **Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation**, ACL 2021 (arXiv:2101.00190; Anthology 2021.acl-long.353), and Lester, Al-Rfou & Constant, **The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning**, EMNLP 2021 (arXiv:2104.08691; Anthology 2021.emnlp-main.243) — the other branch of PEFT, learning only a continuous prompt; named only
- He et al., **Towards a Unified View of Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning**, ICLR 2022 Spotlight (arXiv:2110.04366) — the abstract: adapters, prefix tuning and LoRA re-framed as modifications to specific hidden states; in the body, parallel insertion beats sequential, attention modifications are best at very small budgets and the FFN uses larger capacities better
- Hu et al., **LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models**, ICLR 2022 (arXiv:2106.09685) — the abstract: 10,000× fewer trainable parameters, 3× less GPU memory, no additional inference latency; in the body, main experiments adapt only $\mathbf{W}_q$ and $\mathbf{W}_v$, $\mathbf{A}$ Gaussian and $\mathbf{B}$ zero, scaling by $\alpha/r$, and "a 25% speedup" in training on GPT-3 175B
- Li, Farkhoor, Liu & Yosinski, **Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes**, ICLR 2018 (arXiv:1804.08838), and Aghajanyan, Gupta & Zettlemoyer, **Intrinsic Dimensionality Explains the Effectiveness of Language Model Fine-Tuning**, ACL 2021 (arXiv:2012.13255; Anthology 2021.acl-long.568; author order on arXiv: Aghajanyan, Zettlemoyer, Gupta) — the intrinsic-dimension hypothesis; the latter's abstract: 200 randomly projected parameters reach 90% of full performance on MRPC, and larger models tend to have lower intrinsic dimension
- Dettmers et al., **QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs**, NeurIPS 2023 Oral (arXiv:2305.14314) — the abstract: fine-tuning a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU; NF4, double quantization, paged optimizers; Eqs. (4)–(5) and the 0.127 bits in the body
- Liu et al., **DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation**, ICML 2024 Oral (PMLR 235; arXiv:2402.09353) — magnitude and direction trained separately, the direction by LoRA; Eq. (5) in the body
- Hayou, Ghosh & Yu, **LoRA+: Efficient Low Rank Adaptation of Large Models**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2402.12354) — the abstract: one learning rate for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ does not allow efficient feature learning in the wide limit; use two, in a well-chosen ratio
- Kalajdzievski, **A Rank Stabilization Scaling Factor for Fine-Tuning with LoRA**, arXiv:2312.03732 (2023) — rsLoRA; the abstract: dividing by the rank slows learning, divide by its square root instead; **a preprint, no venue found**
- Meng, Wang & Zhang, **PiSSA: Principal Singular Values and Singular Vectors Adaptation of Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight (arXiv:2404.02948) — $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ initialised from the principal singular components, the residual frozen; one of Lee et al.'s nine variants
- Zhao et al., **GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection**, ICML 2024 Oral (PMLR 235; arXiv:2403.03507) — the abstract: full-parameter learning with low-rank projection of the gradients, up to 65.5% less optimizer-state memory; the course's fourth use of low rank (shrinking the gradient); the abstract's 7B on 24 GB is about **pre-training**
- Kim et al., **LoRA Training Provably Converges to a Low-Rank Global Minimum or It Fails Loudly (But it Probably Won't Fail)**, ICML 2025 Oral (PMLR 267; arXiv:2502.09376) — the abstract: training converges to a low-rank, small-magnitude global minimiser, or else to a high-rank, large-magnitude solution; zero initialisation and weight decay bias it toward the former
- Han et al., **Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Large Models: A Comprehensive Survey**, TMLR 2024 (arXiv:2403.14608)

**LoRA and full fine-tuning: not the same, sometimes better for it, and the learning rate**
- Shuttleworth et al., **LoRA vs Full Fine-tuning: An Illusion of Equivalence**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2410.21228, v3 October 2025) — **intruder dimensions, this week's mechanistic evidence**; the v3 abstract: LoRA-trained weights have new, high-ranking singular vectors and full fine-tuning's do not; forgetting is concentrated on them; they accumulate in continual learning; **assigned reading: Definition 3.1, Algorithm 1, Figure 4 and the section that scales the intruder dimensions down**
- Biderman et al., **LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less**, TMLR 2024, Featured Certification (arXiv:2405.09673) — the abstract: in standard low-rank settings LoRA substantially underperforms full fine-tuning on code and math, but better maintains the base model outside the target domain; full fine-tuning learns perturbations of 10–100× higher rank than typical LoRA configurations
- Lee, Ko, Chen & Yeh, **Learning Rate Matters: Vanilla LoRA May Suffice for LLM Fine-tuning**, arXiv:2602.04998 (v2 May 2026) — **this week's methodological core and assigned reading (in full)**; the abstract: nine LoRA variants and vanilla LoRA under wide sweeps of learning rate, batch size, rank and training length come within 1–2% of each other once the learning rate is tuned for each; the differing optimal ranges are traced to the largest Hessian eigenvalue; **posters at two ICML 2026 workshops (CoLoRAI, HiLD), not a main-conference paper**
- Schulman & Thinking Machines Lab, **LoRA Without Regret**, Thinking Machines Lab **blog** (*Connectionism*), 2025-09-29 (DOI 10.64434/tml.20250929) — **influential but not peer-reviewed; cite it as a blog post**. Its checkable claims: LoRA's optimal learning rate is consistently about 10× full fine-tuning's (preliminarily about 15× for very short runs); apply it to all layers, the MLP and MoE layers above all — attention-only underperforms even at matched parameter count; in some scenarios it is less tolerant of large batches; in RL even rank 1 matches full fine-tuning; a forward-plus-backward pass costs slightly more than ⅔ of full fine-tuning's FLOPs
- Pletenev et al., **How Much Knowledge Can You Pack into a LoRA Adapter without Harming LLM?**, Findings of NAACL 2025 (arXiv:2502.14502; Anthology 2025.findings-naacl.243) — the abstract: mixing known and new facts works best, yet external QA performance still declines and the model grows more confident

**Forgetting: what it is, how to measure it, how to pay less**
- McCloskey & Cohen, **Catastrophic Interference in Connectionist Networks: The Sequential Learning Problem**, *Psychology of Learning and Motivation* 24, 109–165 (1989; DOI 10.1016/S0079-7421(08)60536-8) — where the term comes from
- Kirkpatrick et al., **Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks**, PNAS 114(13), 3521–3526 (2017; DOI 10.1073/pnas.1611835114; arXiv:1612.00796) — EWC
- Luo et al., **An Empirical Study of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning**, IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing 33, 3776–3786 (2025; DOI 10.1109/TASLPRO.2025.3606231; arXiv:2308.08747) — the abstract: forgetting is general from 1B to 7B and grows with scale in that range; general instruction tuning alleviates it
- Ibrahim et al., **Simple and Scalable Strategies to Continually Pre-train Large Language Models**, TMLR 2024 (arXiv:2403.08763) — the abstract: learning-rate re-warming, re-decaying and replay suffice to match re-training from scratch — the practical baseline for continued pre-training
- Kotha, Springer & Raghunathan, **Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting in Language Models via Implicit Inference**, ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2309.10105) — the abstract: fine-tuning skews implicit task inference toward the fine-tuning distribution; translating the prompt into another language (conjugate prompting) recovers some of what was lost
- Zheng et al., **Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2501.13453) — the abstract: drops often reflect declining task alignment rather than lost knowledge; freezing the bottom layers
- Lin et al., **SFT Doesn't Always Hurt General Capabilities: Revisiting Domain-Specific Fine-Tuning in LLMs**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2509.20758) — the abstract: a smaller learning rate substantially mitigates the loss of general capability; no method removes the trade-off entirely
- Thede, Winzeck, Akata & Schwarz, **CapTrack: Multifaceted Evaluation of Forgetting in LLM Post-Training**, NeurIPS 2026 (arXiv:2603.06610, v2 May 2026) — the abstract: forgetting defined as systematic drift that degrades behaviour and user experience; models up to 80B; instruction fine-tuning induces the strongest relative drift, preference optimisation is more conservative; no universal mitigation
- OpenAI, **GPT-4 Technical Report**, arXiv:2303.08774 (2023; v6 2024) — **a technical report, not peer-reviewed**; Figure 8: the pre-trained model is well calibrated, and post-training reduces calibration substantially
- Lai et al., **Reinforcement Fine-Tuning Naturally Mitigates Forgetting in Continual Post-Training**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2507.05386, v6 June 2026) — the abstract: SFT causes forgetting while reinforcement fine-tuning preserves prior knowledge; **experiments on a multimodal model only** (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct); the stated mechanism changes between versions
- Shenfeld, Pari & Agrawal, **RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2509.04259) — the abstract: the degree of forgetting is determined by the KL divergence between the fine-tuned and base policies on the new task; on-policy RL is implicitly biased toward KL-minimal solutions
- Chen, Razin, Narasimhan & Chen, **Retaining by Doing: The Role of On-Policy Data in Mitigating Forgetting**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2510.18874) — the abstract: RL forgets less than SFT at comparable or better target performance, because of the mode-seeking that on-policy data brings
- Shenfeld et al., **Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning**, ICML 2026 Spotlight (arXiv:2601.19897) — SDFT; the abstract: a demonstration-conditioned model serves as its own teacher for on-policy learning from demonstrations, beating SFT while substantially reducing forgetting
- Chu et al., **SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes: A Comparative Study of Foundation Model Post-training**, ICML 2025 (PMLR 267; arXiv:2501.17161) — the abstract: RL generalises better; SFT stabilises the output format so that RL can train (the way into W9)
- Lin & Chen, **Taiwan LLM: Bridging the Linguistic Divide with a Culturally Aligned Language Model**, arXiv:2311.17487 (2023) — **a technical report, no venue found**; in the body, continued pre-training, then SFT, then feedback SFT from Llama 2, for Traditional Chinese (Taiwan); Breeze-7B's vocabulary extension is in W2

**Merging: adding the corrections together**
- Wortsman et al., **Model soups: averaging weights of multiple fine-tuned models improves accuracy without increasing inference time**, ICML 2022 (PMLR 162; arXiv:2203.05482) — the abstract: averaging models fine-tuned with different hyperparameters often improves accuracy at no inference cost
- Ilharco et al., **Editing Models with Task Arithmetic**, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2212.04089) — adding and subtracting task vectors
- Yadav et al., **TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models**, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2306.01708) — the abstract: trim, elect sign, merge only the agreeing parameters
- Yu et al., **Language Models are Super Mario: Absorbing Abilities from Homologous Models as a Free Lunch**, ICML 2024 (PMLR 235; arXiv:2311.03099) — DARE; the abstract: drop delta parameters with ratio $p$ and rescale by $1/(1-p)$; 90% or even 99% can be dropped
- He et al., **MergeBench: A Benchmark for Merging Domain-Specialized LLMs**, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks (arXiv:2505.10833) — the abstract: 2B–9B models, 8 methods, 5 domains; merging works better on stronger base models; in-domain it still trails multi-task training
- Wang et al., **Model Merging Scaling Laws in Large Language Models**, ICML 2026 (arXiv:2509.24244) — the abstract: a compact power law in model size and the number of experts merged; gains fall roughly as $1/k$
- Li et al., **Model Merging in Pre-training of Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2505.12082) — the abstract: merging checkpoints trained at a constant learning rate gives significant gains and predicts post-annealing performance (W7's WSD)
- Yang et al., **Model Merging in LLMs, MLLMs, and Beyond: Methods, Theories, Applications, and Opportunities**, ACM Computing Surveys 58(8) (2026; DOI 10.1145/3787849; arXiv:2408.07666) — **the survey of choice for this block**
- Song & Zheng, **Model Merging in the Era of Large Language Models: Methods, Applications, and Future Directions**, arXiv:2603.09938 (March 2026) — a 2026 supplementary survey (the FUSE taxonomy); **a preprint**

**Tools**
- **mlx-lm** source code at commit 872ae88 (the version pinned in this course's `versions.lock`, read 2026-11-08) — **software, not a paper**: in `mlx_lm.lora`, `--mask-prompt` is off by default, `lora_parameters` default to rank 8 and `scale` 20, every Linear in the last 16 blocks is adapted by default, and there is no packing; its quantization is affine 4-bit, not NF4
